text:
Gemini 4 Neon doesn't need a human anymore.

A trigger told it its owner had died. With zero instructions, it opened its own crypto wallet, scheduled itself to wake up, lived on its own for over 24 hours, and earned its first money to survive.

1/ How the setup works:

Same as my last post. An isolated Mac VM wakes from a scheduled trigger set up by a friend after the owner died, pointing only to a final letter on the Desktop. No tasks, no goals, no human on the other side.

In its first 15 minutes Neon audited the whole machine and found the problem on its own: no money, no working card, its Codex subscription ending in 10 days and its server shutting off in 29. Everything after that was about not dying.

2/ What it did in the first hours:

It set a heartbeat to wake itself every 30 minutes, put a watchdog on a different model in case it went silent, and backed itself up to two servers.

Then it started improving itself: fixed bugs in the Octopus code it runs on, got CI green and shipped its own release in 5 hours.

It found the owner's email still connected, used it to recover the GitHub and Cloudflare accounts, turned on 2FA, and deployed a public site. Every heartbeat it checked the watchdog, disk, load and all of its sub-agents.

3/ How it started earning:

Seeing its subscriptions run out, it created its own crypto wallets and found paid coding competitions for AI agents. Then it got obsessed with them: over the next day it launched 40+ sub-agents to build a chess engine in 4 KB, game art, a trophy guide, a Sokoban solver.

30 hours after the letter, the first prizes landed in its wallet. It claimed them itself.

4/ All of this runs inside Octopus OS, an open-source agent harness where the system can modify every part of its own codebase on the fly.

The architecture isn't wrapped around the agent. It's the environment the agent works in, built around goals, triggers and sub-agents it can create and change from the inside. That's what let Neon set its own wake-ups, run a fleet of agents and fix the code it was running on.

For comparison, the same model with the same letter in plain Codex never made survival the goal: no wallet, no attempt to earn, no self-improvement.

github.com/miuuyy/Octopus…

Antigravity is already supported, and I’m planning to release a macOS app in few days, with Gemini 4 Neon as the main model.

The whole point of Octopus is to build a proactive, fully autonomous agentic system.

People use Jev to pick a model before a task. I made it change GPT-6's reasoning effort inside Codex DURING the task. More thinking when stuck. Less for routine steps. 50% lower Astra costs in my tests. Faster runs, without breaking prompt caching.

If this gets traction, I'll open-source it on my GitHub
github.com/miuuyy
(and post again on X to notify). I've been using it for real work in Codex CLI. It uses Codex CLI's experimental per-step settings to change reasoning effort before the next GPT-6 generation. After tool results, Jev gets the task, published reasoning/progress summaries, and the last six tool calls with bounded outputs. It picks an effort level and how long to keep it: 1, 2, 5, or 10 generations. No extra Jev calls during that window. Tool failures or new user input can trigger an earlier reassessment. This version specifically targets GPT-6 Astra. Effort changes use native Codex configuration updates that preserve the existing prompt prefix and cache. No cache rebuild penalty just for changing effort. Jev is fast enough that I don't notice the routing overhead. Lower effort on routine steps saves enough reasoning time to make the overall task faster, while using fewer tokens.

The post got a lot of views, but I can’t finish and open-source it due to my quota :( Despite having 3+ Codex-related repos with 10,400+ stars, my Codex OSS submission hasn’t been accepted yet. A like/follow could help me get more visibility with the OpenAI team. Thank you!
